unit.name: Socio-Cultural Issues and Sports Psychology
unit.subtitle: Engagement, commercialisation, ethics, sports psychology and the role of physical activity in wellbeing.

common_misconceptions.topic: Antagonistic muscle pairs and the role of the fixator
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name a single muscle as 'the' agonist for a movement without specifying the joint, the direction of movement and which muscle is acting as antagonist. OCR additionally examines the role of the fixator, which AQA does not — students often omit this third role entirely. Content should always frame movement as agonist + antagonist + fixator anchored to a joint and a phase of movement (e.g. biceps agonist, triceps antagonist, deltoid fixator during the up phase of a bicep curl).
common_misconceptions.source: OCR teacher subject web page (https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/) and OCR J587 specification section 1.1.b

common_misconceptions.topic: Lever systems anchored to body locations
common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR pins each lever class to a specific body example (1st = neck, 2nd = ankle, 3rd = elbow). Students who memorise the order LFE without anchoring to OCR's three named body locations lose marks on the 'Identify the lever class operating at the ankle during plantar flexion' question type. Always teach lever class through the spec's three named body examples.

Students identify a sport as 'aerobic' or 'anaerobic' without justifying using duration and intensity. The OCR spec explicitly requires students to 'apply practical examples of aerobic and anaerobic activities in relation to intensity and duration' — justification is the marked content, not the label.

common_misconceptions.topic: Open vs closed skill placement on continua
common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR uses only TWO skill continua (simple-complex difficulty and open-closed environmental). Students confuse 'open' (environment changes) with 'simple' or 'gross' from other boards' continua. Reinforce that OCR only assesses the two continua and that students must justify placement on both — never one without the other.

OCR's 8-mark extended response items use levels-based marking and reward (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) application to physical activity and sport. Students often produce one-sided answers or forget to apply each point to a named sporting context. Encourage 'On one hand... However...' structures with a sporting worked example anchored to each point.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR teacher support — assessment of extended response, J587 specification section 3h

common_misconceptions.misconception: OCR's SMART acronym is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. Students who learn the more common 'Realistic' or 'Time-bound' variant (used by other boards) lose definition marks. Drill the OCR-specific letters from lesson 7 onwards and reinforce in flashcards.

student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Evaluate: OCR's top-tier extended response is 8 marks (not 9 like AQA). Students often produce one-sided arguments and forget to apply each point to a named sport. The mark scheme is levels-based and rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sustained sporting application. Encourage 'For X... However Y...' paragraphs each anchored to a sporting example.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Analyse: Students list rather than analyse. Each point should be developed: state the factor, link it to performance, give a sporting example. Avoid bullet-point answers; encourage continuous prose.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Interpret Data: OCR explicitly tests data interpretation across both papers (use-of-data symbol marks the spec sections). Students copy numbers from the table without saying what they show. Always make a comparison, quote one figure, then explain the sporting implication.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Calculate from Data: Students forget the unit (e.g. bpm, %, seconds, l/min) or skip showing working. Mark schemes typically award one mark for working, one for the correct figure, one for the unit. Always show all three. Note: OCR allows a calculator on Paper 1.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State Two: Students give two near-identical answers (e.g. 'increased heart rate' and 'heart rate goes up'). Mark schemes award once for the same physiological point — the second answer must be qualitatively different.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 01 (Physical factors affecting performance) is 30% of the qualification = 60 marks. Applied anatomy and physiology dominates this paper — every paper carries multi-mark questions on muscles, the cardio-respiratory system and the effects of exercise. Treat the first 9 lessons of unit 1 as the foundation block and revisit them in worked examples in later lessons (training, warm up, injury prevention).

Component 02 (Socio-cultural issues and sports psychology) is 30% of the qualification = 60 marks. Topics divide roughly equally between socio-cultural (engagement, commercialisation, ethics, drugs, violence) and sports psychology (skill, goals, mental preparation, guidance, feedback) plus the wellbeing strand. Allocate practice questions evenly across the two strands.

Use of data appears across both papers, marked in the OCR spec with the data-handling symbol. Bake data interpretation into practice questions throughout the build, not just into dedicated data lessons. Topics flagged for data: short-term and long-term effects of exercise, components of fitness, health/fitness/wellbeing, engagement patterns.

Socio-cultural and ethical issues (commercialisation, drugs, player violence) yield rich 6- and 8-mark questions. These lessons need contemporary, balanced examples with explicit positive and negative impacts framed.

Practical (Component 04) and Analysis & Evaluation (Component 05) together make up 40% of the qualification — 60 marks + 20 marks of NEA — but are teacher-assessed and not addressed by this revision platform. Students are pointed to their school's PE department for activity assessment and the analysis-and-evaluation coursework. The 27 lessons in this plan cover 100% of the assessable theory content for Components 01 and 02 (60% of the qualification).
current_spec_changes: OCR J587 specification version 1.7 (January 2024) is the current authoritative document. No content additions or removals affect the theory papers for the 2026 series. Source: https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/specification-at-a-glance/

OCR's NEA approved-activities list is updated periodically. Practical changes do not affect theory content. Refer to the OCR Guide to NEA in Physical Education for current approved activities. Source: https://www.ocr.org.uk/qualifications/gcse/physical-education-j587-from-2016/
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance on retrieval practice: the active attempt to recall is what builds long-term memory; quizzes must include a delay between learning and recall, balance challenge with success, and provide feedback. Knowledge checks and flashcards in this build must be true retrieval tasks (not just re-reading) and should mix anatomy, training and socio-cultural content to force students to discriminate between related concepts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-not-another-quiz-refining-retrieval-practice

EEF cognitive science review identifies dual coding (pairing words with diagrams) as a high-utility classroom strategy. PE content is anatomy-heavy: where a diagram would clarify (heart chambers, lever systems anchored to neck/ankle/elbow, planes/axes), the lesson should describe it precisely in text and include a key-fact 'sketch this without looking' retrieval prompt. Free-tier lessons do not embed generated images, so the prose must do the imaging work. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/evidence-reviews/cognitive-science-approaches-in-the-classroom

EEF spaced-practice principle: revisiting material across days outperforms massed practice. Lessons should explicitly cross-reference earlier lessons (e.g. when teaching warm-up, retrieve the cardio-respiratory and muscular adaptations from lessons 6 and 9). Build deliberate retrieval prompts into key-facts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-putting-cognitive-science-principles-into-practice

EEF interleaving principle: mixing related topics in retrieval forces students to discriminate. Knowledge checks should not be pure single-topic — Component 01 lessons should mix anatomy with training, and Component 02 lessons should mix sports psychology with socio-cultural influences. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-the-abc-of-cognitive-science

Glossary terms: PE is terminology-dense (every named bone, muscle, joint, training method, principle and ethical concept needs precise definition). Aim for at least 6 inline glossary terms per lesson; 8–10 is realistic in anatomy lessons. Definitions should be one sentence and reusable across lessons.

Data interpretation: OCR Paper 1 and Paper 2 both test use of data. Generate ORIGINAL fictional data tables and graph descriptions in question stems — never reproduce real OCR figures. Use realistic numbers (e.g. 'Liam's heart rate during a 30-min run: rest 70 bpm, peak 165 bpm, recovery 90 bpm at 5 min'). Include at least one '4 marks — Interpret Data' or '3 marks — Calculate from Data' question in lessons where the topic is amenable (Cardiovascular System, Effects of Exercise, Components of Fitness, Engagement Patterns, Health/Fitness/Wellbeing, Diet and Nutrition). Source: OCR J587 specification, use-of-data symbol marking.

Mark scheme rubric: StudyVault uses Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging on 6- and 8-mark levels-based questions. NEVER use 'Level 1/2/3', 'Nothing worthy of credit' or 'Award X marks for Y'. Phrase mark allocations as '1 mark for X; 1 mark for Y' or 'Up to 3 marks: identification (1), context (1), explanation (1)'. The validator hard-bans the 'Award N marks for' pattern.

Plain-text fields (description, practice_questions[].text/.type/.marks, knowledge_checks[].q, flashcard_questions[].q/.a, glossary_terms[].term/.definition) MUST use plain unicode (apostrophes, en-dashes, em-dashes typed directly). NEVER use HTML entities such as ’, &, – in these fields — entities are only allowed inside content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html.

Copyright: do not include spec codes (J587), paper codes (J587/01, J587/02), section labels, or OCR's trademark question stems verbatim. Do not write 'Other than X, identify...' style questions that mimic OCR's structure. Do not reproduce OCR mark scheme phrasing. Build generic GCSE-level questions with our 11 registered command-word types.

lessons_in_batch.title: Types of Feedback in Sport
lessons_in_batch.description: Intrinsic, extrinsic, knowledge of performance, knowledge of results, positive and negative feedback.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Six named feedback types match AQA's almost exactly. Re-spec to 2.2 and tweak examples to OCR-favoured contexts. Worked examples should pair beginner-vs-elite scenarios.

lessons_in_batch.title: Health, Fitness and Wellbeing
lessons_in_batch.description: Defining health, fitness and wellbeing and the physical, emotional and social benefits of sport.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR places this in Paper 2 (component 02), where AQA placed it in the wellbeing block of Paper 2 too. OCR's named outcomes are more explicit: physical (CHD, BP, bone density, obesity, T2 diabetes, posture, fitness), emotional (self-esteem, stress management, image), social (friendship, belonging, loneliness). AQA was looser. Restructure around OCR's named lists; add age-group application as OCR explicitly tests 'apply to different age groups'.

lessons_in_batch.title: Sedentary Lifestyle and Consequences
lessons_in_batch.description: What a sedentary lifestyle is and how inactivity contributes to obesity, CHD, diabetes and poor wellbeing.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR does NOT include somatotypes (ectomorph/mesomorph/endomorph) — that's AQA-only. Strip somatotypes entirely and refocus on the spec's 'consequences of a sedentary lifestyle' learning outcome with the named conditions (obesity, CHD, T2 diabetes, hypertension, low self-esteem, loneliness). OCR also explicitly tests data response on health/fitness/wellbeing — bake in a data interpretation question.

lessons_in_batch.title: Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons_in_batch.description: Components of a balanced diet, the role of macronutrients and the effect of hydration on performance.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OCR's seven named diet components (carbs, proteins, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre, water/hydration) match AQA closely. Drop AQA's calorie-calculation depth (Kcal computations, daily energy need maths) — OCR only requires understanding of energy use, not calculation. Keep hydration and dehydration content.
